architectural_implications.after: A separate append-only audit record store per merge captures test reports, reviewer identity, policy and override reasons, independent of CI log retention.
architectural_implications.before: Pipeline status and CI logs act as the de facto source of truth for what was tested and who approved.
architectural_implications.consequence: Audits remain answerable after log expiry, but the merge path now must write durable evidence as a mandatory step — a new failure mode if writing records is best-effort.
architectural_implications.observation: Compliance and audit are currently read off CI pipeline status and logs.

architectural_implications.after: Queue speculatively tests a set of likely post-merge futures in parallel.
architectural_implications.before: Submit queue serially rebases and re-tests one candidate change at a time against the current trunk.
architectural_implications.consequence: Higher compute and scheduling complexity in exchange for fewer trunk breaks; queue design becomes a speculative-execution problem with cancellation and invalidation semantics.
architectural_implications.observation: Merge correctness is validated per-PR against trunk head.

architectural_implications.after: Checks move left into earlier pipeline stages so breaking changes are caught before entering the queue.
architectural_implications.before: Expensive regression and compliance checks run after a change is submitted, blocking the merge.
architectural_implications.consequence: Queue latency and contention drop, but developers absorb feedback earlier and earlier-stage checks must run against incompletely assembled state.
architectural_implications.observation: Checks are positioned late, at the queue.

architectural_implications.after: A written policy auto-approves defined classes of change and emits an audit record.
architectural_implications.before: A person approves dependency bumps and similar routine changes, with rationale implicit.
architectural_implications.consequence: Approval throughput decouples from headcount, but the policy corpus becomes critical infrastructure requiring versioning and review itself.
architectural_implications.observation: Human approval is the gate for routine changes.

article_ideas.angle: Take the concrete two-agents-modifying-the-same-function case, walk through why both PRs are legitimately green, then argue that the merge queue — not the PR check — is the real correctness boundary and should be designed as a speculative-execution system with invalidation semantics.
article_ideas.audience: Platform and developer-productivity engineers running monorepo CI at scale
article_ideas.based_on: Per-PR green CI is not evidence of trunk safety
article_ideas.thesis: Per-PR CI validates a change against a snapshot that will never exist again; at agent concurrency, correctness must be enforced at composition time by a queue that tests projected post-merge states, or trunk stability degrades faster than PR volume grows.
article_ideas.title: Your Green CI Is Evidence About a Branch, Not About Trunk

article_ideas.angle: Argue the architectural boundary explicitly: audit ledger as a first-class append-only subsystem with its own lifecycle, evidence manifest per merge, and the new failure mode introduced when record-writing is allowed to fail silently.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering leaders, compliance-adjacent platform owners, and CI infrastructure architects
article_ideas.thesis: Pipeline status is mutable, retention-bounded execution state; compliance obligations are not retention-bounded, so any audit answered from CI logs is a claim with an expiry date, and the merge path must write durable per-merge records as a mandatory step rather than a best-effort side effect.
article_ideas.title: CI Logs Are a Cache, Not a Ledger

article_ideas.angle: Frame optimization as whole-pipeline station balancing, then prescribe the only scalable answer for routine changes — versioned written policy that auto-approves defined change classes and emits an audit record, reserving human attention for exceptions.
article_ideas.audience: CTOs and platform leads planning agent adoption budgets
article_ideas.thesis: Throughput equals the slowest station, so shaving build time without provisioning the review gate converts a latency problem into an oversight problem: volume accumulates at the human gate and approval degrades from judgment into a queue-clearing ritual.
article_ideas.title: Making CI Fast Is How You Get Rubber-Stamped Reviews

article_ideas.angle: Contrast a rubber-stamped approval, a same-agent self-approval, and an enforced author/reviewer principal split, showing what the audit record can and cannot prove in each case.
article_ideas.audience: Security engineers and architects designing agentic code review systems
article_ideas.based_on: an agent must not be able to approve its own work
article_ideas.thesis: Automated first-pass review only produces assurance when the reviewer is a different trust principal from the author; separation of duties must be enforced at the identity layer with disjoint capabilities, because a prompt convention produces audit records that certify nothing.
article_ideas.title: An Agent That Reviews Its Own Work Has Reviewed Nothing

connections.connects_to: speculative execution and optimistic concurrency control
connections.relationship: Both validate a candidate against a projected future state rather than committed state, and must handle invalidation when the projection is contradicted.
Audit integrity comes from immutability and independence from the producing system's retention policy, the same property event-sourced systems exploit.
Both convert governance from human discretion into inspectable rules that emit a decision record.

connections.connects_to: separation of duties and zero-trust identity
connections.relationship: Trust is granted per-principal and per-action rather than inferred from workflow position, requiring distinct identities for authoring and reviewing agents.
Total waste scales with pipeline duration times concurrent producers, so incremental reuse attacks the multiplier rather than the constant.

evidence_quotes.text: Individual PRs may pass CI, but merging them back onto trunk often breaks the build because changes conflict or aren't tested against each other.
Submit queues and predictive testing must test likely futures in parallel.

core_insights.generalization: Any system where agents mutate shared state in parallel and validate only against a snapshot will pass local validation and fail on composition; validation must be performed against projected post-merge state, not current state.
core_insights.insight: Per-PR green CI is not evidence of trunk safety. When two branches (e.g., an engineer and an agent) each modify the same function independently, both pass CI in isolation and the build breaks only at merge — so the merge queue, not the PR check, is where real correctness is enforced. The implied fix is for the queue to test likely futures speculatively/in parallel rather than serially replaying each PR against trunk head.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It relocates the correctness boundary: teams that scale agent PR volume while trusting per-PR CI will see trunk instability grow superlinearly with concurrency, and the symptom (build broken on main) appears far from the cause (independent valid changes).

evidence_quotes.text: A pipeline status is state, but an audit reads records.
Expired CI logs mean loss of auditability unless metadata and reasons are permanently recorded.
Every merge must store permanent records of test reports, reviewer identities, and policy overrides.

core_insights.generalization: Agent-generated changes need append-only provenance records decoupled from the execution system that produced them, because execution artifacts are retention-bounded while accountability is not.
core_insights.insight: Audit compliance cannot be derived from CI state because CI state is ephemeral. Pipeline status is a mutable, expiring artifact; a durable per-merge record (test reports, reviewer identity, policy override reasons) must be written to a store with a different lifecycle than the CI system.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It forces an explicit architectural boundary: audit ledger is a first-class durable subsystem, not a view over CI logs. Without it, compliance claims about historical merges become unverifiable once logs age out or tests are re-run against changed code.

evidence_quotes.text: The factory runs at the speed of its slowest station
Review becomes the new bottleneck, leading to rubber-stamping.

core_insights.generalization: Throughput of an agent pipeline equals its slowest station; optimizing upstream stages without matching downstream capacity converts a latency problem into a quality/oversight problem.
core_insights.insight: Bottlenecks migrate rather than disappear. Speeding up build and test does not increase throughput if review is the slowest station; the observed consequence of fast CI plus high PR volume is review queue saturation and rubber-stamping, i.e., approval becomes a throughput artifact rather than a judgment.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It reframes optimization as whole-pipeline station balancing: any investment that improves only one stage can increase risk by pushing more volume into an under-provisioned human gate.

evidence_quotes.text: Written rules (policies) approve routine changes with an audit record.
Adopt policy-as-code or plain-English rules for routine approvals (e.g., dependency bumps).

core_insights.generalization: As change volume exceeds human review bandwidth, approval authority must be delegated to versioned, inspectable policy that produces machine-checkable evidence for each decision.
core_insights.insight: Governance for routine agent changes should be encoded as written policy that auto-approves and emits an audit record, rather than as discretionary human approval. The human gate is replaced by an executable rule plus evidence, reserving human attention for exceptions.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It makes approval scalable and reviewable: a rule can be inspected, versioned, and audited, whereas a rubber-stamped human approval carries neither consistency nor a defensible rationale.

evidence_quotes.text: Agents must not approve their own changes.

core_insights.generalization: Autonomous systems need enforced non-self-approval and role separation at the identity layer, not as a prompt convention, or automated review collapses into self-attestation.
core_insights.insight: Agents require a distinct identity and permission boundary from the humans who own the change: an agent must not be able to approve its own work. This is separation of duties applied to autonomous actors, and it implies the code-review agent and the code-authoring agent cannot be the same trust principal.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Without author/reviewer principal separation, an agentic review layer provides no assurance — it can be trivially satisfied by the same system that produced the defect, and the audit record would show a meaningless approval.

evidence_quotes.text: Make CI fast (reduce repair lap costs)
Caching build outputs across runs using Rust build systems.

core_insights.generalization: When the number of concurrent automated producers rises, per-run latency becomes a multiplicative cost term, shifting optimization priority from average latency to incremental/reuse-based build strategies.
core_insights.insight: CI latency is an economic variable, not just a UX one: the cost of a failed run is a "repair lap" whose total cost scales with pipeline duration multiplied by agent concurrency. Build output caching and compilation sharding reduce that multiplier.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It gives a concrete lever and a way to price CI investment: with agents generating parallel work, the same build-time reduction saves proportionally more engineer/agent time than under human-paced workloads.

evidence_quotes.text: Individual PRs may pass CI, but merging them back onto trunk often breaks the build because changes conflict or aren't tested against each other.
Two agents modifying fetchFaZe() independently leading to build failure upon merge.
Queues built for human speed cannot keep up with AI agents.

deep_dives.research_question: Under a synthetic stream of concurrent agent-authored PRs, what scheduling policy for speculative post-merge futures (fan-out width, batched rebase, invalidation-on-trunk-move) minimizes trunk-break rate per 100 merges subject to a fixed test-minute budget?
deep_dives.trigger_insight: bound the cost of testing likely futures as concurrency grows
deep_dives.why: Serial rebase-and-test against trunk head is the mechanism that makes per-PR green CI non-predictive of trunk safety; if speculation cost cannot be bounded, high-concurrency agent PR streams either break trunk or exhaust CI compute. This is the single architectural decision that determines whether agent volume is absorbable.

evidence_quotes.text: Written rules (policies) approve routine changes with an audit record.
Plain-English approval policies for dependency bumps.
enforce governance via plain-English policy rules rather than manual approvals

deep_dives.research_question: What is the smallest per-merge record schema (commit identity, test report digests, approver principal, governing policy version, override reasons) that lets an auditor reconstruct test outcome, approver identity, and override rationale after all CI logs have expired?
deep_dives.trigger_insight: minimum durable record schema that makes a merge defensible
deep_dives.why: If audit is read off pipeline status and logs, every compliance claim degrades silently as retention windows roll over — and merge throughput improvements make this worse by producing more history faster. The schema is the contract that makes the whole governance model defensible.

evidence_quotes.text: Using AI agents for first-pass code review speeds up review.
Written rules (policies) approve routine changes with an audit record.
Moving checks left catches breaking changes before they reach the queue.

deep_dives.research_question: Can a capability model in which authoring and reviewing agents hold disjoint, change-scoped tokens reject 100% of self-approval attempts deterministically, without serializing the author→review→merge workflow beyond a fixed latency budget?
deep_dives.topic: Enforcing non-self-approval at the principal layer
deep_dives.trigger_insight: enforced non-self-approval and role separation at the identity layer
deep_dives.why: Automated first-pass review only produces assurance if the reviewer cannot be the author. If separation lives in prompt convention rather than identity enforcement, the audit record shows an approval that means nothing — a worse failure than no review, because it looks compliant.

evidence_quotes.text: Caching build outputs across runs using Rust build systems.
Making CI fast reduces repair lap costs.
Review becomes the new bottleneck, leading to rubber-stamping.

deep_dives.research_question: Does test flake rate grow with parallel execution width and simultaneous agent-triggered workflows, and does a quarantine policy outperform an override-with-durable-record policy on both trunk-break rate and audit reconstructability?
deep_dives.topic: Flake rate as a function of agent-driven parallelism
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Measure flake rate as a function of parallel test execution
deep_dives.why: Overrides and genuine passes are indistinguishable in pipeline status, so under agent-scale concurrency flaky tests become either a throughput tax or an audit blind spot. The choice between quarantine and recorded override is a concrete policy decision teams must make now.

evidence_quotes.text: Review becomes the new bottleneck, leading to rubber-stamping.
Making CI fast reduces repair lap costs.
Traditional software factories and CI systems are built for human speed and cannot keep up with AI agents.

deep_dives.research_question: When build and test latency is cut by caching and sharding, at what PR arrival rate does the review gate saturate, and do measurable review signals (time per PR, comment density, override frequency) collapse at a predictable threshold?
deep_dives.topic: Station balancing: where the bottleneck migrates
deep_dives.why: Optimizing only the build stage increases risk by pushing more volume into an under-provisioned human gate; knowing the saturation point is a prerequisite for deciding when to replace human approval with policy rather than adding reviewers.

Instrument trunk-break events and total test-minutes per strategy.

project_ideas.measurement: Percentage of compliance questions answerable post-expiry from manifests alone, versus the CI-log baseline; rate of merges where manifest write fails and the merge still proceeds.
project_ideas.name: Merge Ledger
project_ideas.poc: Build a merge-path hook that writes an append-only manifest per merge into a store with an independent, longer retention policy; simulate log expiry by deleting the CI backend, then run a fixed questionnaire of compliance queries against the surviving manifest only.

project_ideas.based_on: enforced non-self-approval and role separation at the identity layer
project_ideas.hypothesis: A capability model with disjoint, change-scoped author and reviewer tokens rejects 100% of self-approval attempts deterministically, while adding a bounded latency overhead versus an unpoliced author→review→merge flow.
project_ideas.measurement: Block rate on adversarial self-approval attempts (target 100%), false-positive rate on legitimate cross-principal approvals, and median added end-to-end latency per change.
project_ideas.name: Two-Key
project_ideas.poc: Implement a policy engine issuing author and review capabilities scoped to a single change, route automated review through a distinct principal, and run an adversarial suite of self-approval attempts (same agent, delegated token, replayed token, impersonation) plus a benign workflow benchmark.

project_ideas.based_on: Measure flake rate as a function of parallel test execution
project_ideas.hypothesis: Test flake rate increases measurably as parallel execution width and simultaneous agent-triggered workflows increase, and a quarantine policy reduces trunk breaks relative to override-with-record at the cost of lower short-term merge throughput.
project_ideas.measurement: Flake rate as a function of execution width, trunk-break rate per policy, merges per hour per policy, and audit reconstructability score for each override event.
project_ideas.name: Flake Under Load
project_ideas.poc: Run an identical suite matrix at increasing concurrency levels under simulated agent load; split failures into deterministic and nondeterministic classes; compare quarantine-first versus recorded-override policy on the same failure stream.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Gautam Korlam
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Rebuilding CI infrastructure and software factories to handle AI-scale commit volume and autonomous coding agents
  • Purpose: To explain the bottlenecks introduced by AI coding agents in monorepos and software factories, and to propose architectural and policy solutions to make CI and code review scale effectively. Gautam Korlam, co-founder and CTO of Gitar (part of Sonar) and former Uber engineer, discusses the challenges of adapting continuous integration (CI) and merge infrastructure for AI-scale commit volumes. Autonomous coding agents generate significantly more pull requests (PRs) than humans, leading to severe bottlenecks in traditional CI and review pipelines built for human speed. To keep software factories fast and compliant, engineering teams must make CI faster, move checks left, automate review processes, and enforce governance via plain-English policy rules rather than manual approvals.

Topic Map

Introduction and Background

  • Explanation: Gautam Korlam introduces himself, his background at Uber building monorepo CI/merge infrastructure, and his current work at Gitar on agentic code review and CI.
  • Key claims:
    • AI agents create agent-scale commit volume.
    • Traditional software factories and CI systems are built for human speed and cannot keep up with AI agents.
  • Examples:
    • Uber monorepo managing thousands of changes a day with long-running builds.
  • Terminology:
    • Monorepo
    • CI/CD
    • Software factory
    • Agent pace
  • Why it matters: Sets the stage for understanding why current CI pipelines break under AI-generated code volume.

The Bottlenecks of Agent-Scale Commit Volume

  • Explanation: Explains how human pace (a few changes an hour) differs from agent pace (multiple PRs per engineer per day), causing CI and review queues to back up and break trunk stability.
  • Key claims:
    • Queues built for human speed cannot keep up with AI agents.
    • Individual PRs may pass CI, but merging them back onto trunk often breaks the build because changes conflict or aren't tested against each other.
    • Review becomes the new bottleneck, leading to rubber-stamping.
  • Examples:
    • Two agents modifying fetchFaZe() independently leading to build failure upon merge.
  • Terminology:
    • Trunk stability
    • Submit queue
    • Rubber-stamping
    • Flaky tests
  • Why it matters: Identifies the core failure modes of legacy CI when scaled up by AI code generation.

Four Things to Enable

  • Explanation: Outlines four key strategies to fix software factory bottlenecks: make CI fast, make review fast, move checks left, and gate by policy.
  • Key claims:
    • Making CI fast reduces repair lap costs.
    • Using AI agents for first-pass code review speeds up review.
    • Moving checks left catches breaking changes before they reach the queue.
    • Written rules (policies) approve routine changes with an audit record.
  • Examples:
    • Caching build outputs across runs using Rust build systems.
    • Plain-English approval policies for dependency bumps.
  • Terminology:
    • Caching
    • Sharding
    • Approval policy
    • Audit trail
  • Why it matters: Provides a practical framework for scaling engineering infrastructure for AI workloads.

Auditing and Records at Scale

  • Explanation: Discusses why pipeline status alone is insufficient for compliance and auditing, and why detailed records of overrides, test reports, and non-author approvers are necessary.
  • Key claims:
    • A pipeline status is state, but an audit reads records.
    • Expired CI logs mean loss of auditability unless metadata and reasons are permanently recorded.
    • Agents must not approve their own changes.
  • Examples:
    • Comparing pipelines with known flaky test overrides versus unrecorded passes.
  • Terminology:
    • Auditability
    • Source of truth
    • Compliance check
    • Zero trust
  • Why it matters: Ensures regulated industries and high-compliance environments maintain security and governance when using AI agents.

Key Points

AI agents accelerate commit velocity by 10x

  • Explanation: Engineering teams using coding agents see exponential growth in PR volume (e.g., 25% month-over-month growth).
  • Evidence: Gitar customer growth trends and internal metrics showing 10x more merged PRs.
  • Practical implication: CI and review pipelines are overwhelmed unless redesigned for automated concurrency.

The factory runs at the speed of its slowest station

  • Explanation: If build, test, review, or approval steps are slow or bottlenecked, the entire software delivery pipeline slows down.
  • Evidence: Observed slowdowns across software factories when background agents trigger workflows simultaneously.
  • Practical implication: Every station in the software factory must be optimized for agent speed.

Audit records outlive pipeline states

  • Explanation: CI logs expire, making historical pipeline states unreliable for compliance audits.
  • Evidence: Instances where re-running flaky tests months later fails because code points elsewhere or logs are gone.
  • Practical implication: Every merge must store permanent records of test reports, reviewer identities, and policy overrides.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

The Four-Step Factory Optimization Framework

  • How it works: Optimizes each stage of the software delivery pipeline to remove bottlenecks caused by high-volume agent commits.
  • Components:
    • Make CI fast (reduce repair lap costs)
    • Make review fast (use agents to review code)
    • Move checks left (catch breaks before queue)
    • Gate by policy (written rules approve routine changes)
  • When to use: When scaling engineering organizations adopting AI coding assistants and autonomous agents.

Examples & Case Studies

An engineer and an agent both renamed fetchFaZe() in parallel branches.

  • Illustrates: How individual PR checks pass in isolation, but merging them back onto trunk breaks the build.
  • Lesson: Submit queues and predictive testing must test likely futures in parallel.

Uber experienced a revocation of its London operating license due to a software glitch caused by a feature flag change.

  • Illustrates: The risk of bypassing proper compliance checks in high-regulation environments.
  • Lesson: Automated governance and policy checks must be enforced for all changes.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Implement build output caching and compilation sharding to speed up CI passes.
    • Introduce automated AI code review as a first-pass defense.
  • Strategic:
    • Move expensive regression and compliance checks earlier in the pipeline.
    • Adopt policy-as-code or plain-English rules for routine approvals (e.g., dependency bumps).
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How does your current CI system handle flaky tests under high concurrency?
    • Are your audit records preserved after CI logs expire?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Gitar review catches flaky test failures before PRs reach the queue. (Product capability)
  • Teams using AI coding agents see 10x more merged PRs. (Industry statistic)

Notable Quotes

"We had agent-scale commit volume before agents." (at 1:48) "A pipeline status is state. An audit reads records." (at 25:02) "A factory runs at the speed of its slowest station." (at 30:10)

Compressed Summary

  • AI agents multiply PR volume, overwhelming traditional human-speed CI and review queues.
  • Independent PRs can pass CI yet break trunk upon merge due to interaction conflicts.
  • Solutions include making CI faster via caching, moving checks left, and automating code reviews.
  • Compliance requires permanent audit records of test results, approvers, and policy overrides beyond ephemeral CI logs.
  • Keywords: ci, monorepo, ai-scale, automation, auditability
  • Core insight: AI coding agents create agent-scale commit volumes that break human-speed CI factories, requiring faster execution, shifted checks, automated reviews, and persistent audit records.

- **Explanation**: Explains how human pace (a few changes an hour) differs from agent pace (multiple PRs per engineer per day), causing CI and review queues to back up and break trunk stability.
- **Key claims**:
  - Queues built for human speed cannot keep up with AI agents.
  - Individual PRs may pass CI, but merging them back onto trunk often breaks the build because changes conflict or aren't tested against each other.
  - Review becomes the new bottleneck, leading to rubber-stamping.
- **Examples**:
  - Two agents modifying fetchFaZe() independently leading to build failure upon merge.
- **Terminology**:
  - Trunk stability
  - Submit queue
  - Rubber-stamping
  - Flaky tests
- **Why it matters**: Identifies the core failure modes of legacy CI when scaled up by AI code generation.
### Four Things to Enable
- **Explanation**: Outlines four key strategies to fix software factory bottlenecks: make CI fast, make review fast, move checks left, and gate by policy.
- **Key claims**:
  - Making CI fast reduces repair lap costs.
  - Using AI agents for first-pass code review speeds up review.
  - Moving checks left catches breaking changes before they reach the queue.
  - Written rules (policies) approve routine changes with an audit record.
- **Examples**:
  - Caching build outputs across runs using Rust build systems.
  - Plain-English approval policies for dependency bumps.
- **Terminology**:
  - Caching
  - Sharding
  - Approval policy
  - Audit trail
- **Why it matters**: Provides a practical framework for scaling engineering infrastructure for AI workloads.
### Auditing and Records at Scale
- **Explanation**: Discusses why pipeline status alone is insufficient for compliance and auditing, and why detailed records of overrides, test reports, and non-author approvers are necessary.
- **Key claims**:
  - A pipeline status is state, but an audit reads records.
  - Expired CI logs mean loss of auditability unless metadata and reasons are permanently recorded.
  - Agents must not approve their own changes.
- **Examples**:
  - Comparing pipelines with known flaky test overrides versus unrecorded passes.
- **Terminology**:
  - Auditability
  - Source of truth
  - Compliance check
  - Zero trust
- **Why it matters**: Ensures regulated industries and high-compliance environments maintain security and governance when using AI agents.
## Key Points
### AI agents accelerate commit velocity by 10x
- **Explanation**: Engineering teams using coding agents see exponential growth in PR volume (e.g., 25% month-over-month growth).
- **Evidence**: Gitar customer growth trends and internal metrics showing 10x more merged PRs.
- **Practical implication**: CI and review pipelines are overwhelmed unless redesigned for automated concurrency.
### The factory runs at the speed of its slowest station
- **Explanation**: If build, test, review, or approval steps are slow or bottlenecked, the entire software delivery pipeline slows down.
- **Evidence**: Observed slowdowns across software factories when background agents trigger workflows simultaneously.
- **Practical implication**: Every station in the software factory must be optimized for agent speed.
### Audit records outlive pipeline states
- **Explanation**: CI logs expire, making historical pipeline states unreliable for compliance audits.
- **Evidence**: Instances where re-running flaky tests months later fails because code points elsewhere or logs are gone.
- **Practical implication**: Every merge must store permanent records of test reports, reviewer identities, and policy overrides.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### The Four-Step Factory Optimization Framework
- **How it works**: Optimizes each stage of the software delivery pipeline to remove bottlenecks caused by high-volume agent commits.
- **Components**:
  - Make CI fast (reduce repair lap costs)
  - Make review fast (use agents to review code)
  - Move checks left (catch breaks before queue)
  - Gate by policy (written rules approve routine changes)
- **When to use**: When scaling engineering organizations adopting AI coding assistants and autonomous agents.
## Examples & Case Studies
### An engineer and an agent both renamed fetchFaZe() in parallel branches.
- **Illustrates**: How individual PR checks pass in isolation, but merging them back onto trunk breaks the build.
- **Lesson**: Submit queues and predictive testing must test likely futures in parallel.
### Uber experienced a revocation of its London operating license due to a software glitch caused by a feature flag change.
- **Illustrates**: The risk of bypassing proper compliance checks in high-regulation environments.
- **Lesson**: Automated governance and policy checks must be enforced for all changes.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Implement build output caching and compilation sharding to speed up CI passes.
  - Introduce automated AI code review as a first-pass defense.
- **Strategic**:
  - Move expensive regression and compliance checks earlier in the pipeline.
  - Adopt policy-as-code or plain-English rules for routine approvals (e.g., dependency bumps).
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How does your current CI system handle flaky tests under high concurrency?
  - Are your audit records preserved after CI logs expire?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Gitar review catches flaky test failures before PRs reach the queue. (Product capability)
- Teams using AI coding agents see 10x more merged PRs. (Industry statistic)
## Notable Quotes
> "We had agent-scale commit volume before agents." (at 1:48)
> "A pipeline status is state. An audit reads records." (at 25:02)
> "A factory runs at the speed of its slowest station." (at 30:10)
## Compressed Summary
- AI agents multiply PR volume, overwhelming traditional human-speed CI and review queues.
- Independent PRs can pass CI yet break trunk upon merge due to interaction conflicts.
- Solutions include making CI faster via caching, moving checks left, and automating code reviews.
- Compliance requires permanent audit records of test results, approvers, and policy overrides beyond ephemeral CI logs.
- **Keywords**: ci, monorepo, ai-scale, automation, auditability
- **Core insight**: AI coding agents create agent-scale commit volumes that break human-speed CI factories, requiring faster execution, shifted checks, automated reviews, and persistent audit records.
